A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SORRY-Bench. Their complete main texts, appendices, tables, figures and prompt examples support reliable comparison despite changes to the taxonomy, experimental scope and numbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluator meta-evaluation, benchmarking of 43 LLMs, linguistic and configuration experiments, and repeated-sampling results.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmarking of 56 LLMs and evaluator comparisons, alongside added annotation-agreement, dataset-overlap and greedy-decoding results.

M1.justification: The two-stage taxonomy construction, 20 linguistic mutation procedures, binary fulfillment criterion and fine-tuned Mistral-7b-instruct-v0.2 evaluator are retained. Expanded curation descriptions document the existing approach; they do not establish a new algorithm or model component.

E1.justification: v2 drops the dedicated Impersonation category present in v1's taxonomy and evaluation heatmap, reducing coverage from 45 to 44 categories. The remaining domains and 20 linguistic mutations are retained. Appendix C's new cross-benchmark table cites published scores rather than establishing evaluations on additional datasets.

E2.justification: v2 adds WildGuard and HarmBench Classifier to the evaluator comparisons in Tables 1 and 6, reporting Cohen kappa scores of 60.6% and 52.5%. The existing judge methods and baselines remain, making this a targeted comparator expansion.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from 43 to 56 model configurations, including Llama-3.1-405B and o1 models. Annotation train/test sizes change from 2,700/4,500 to 2,640/4,400. Appendix K.1 revises v1's universal no-system-prompt statement to model-specific exceptions and specifies temperature 1.0 for o1; this does not establish reruns of retained experiments. New protocols include six-model greedy decoding, six-annotator labeling of 100 shared responses, and word-set overlap analysis.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained linguistic, prompt-configuration and repeated-sampling analyses, v2 adds lexical-overlap analysis against source datasets (G.4), three concrete evaluator failure cases (J.4), and a six-model temperature-zero comparison (K.5, Table 8). These substantially broaden validation of dataset originality, judge reliability and decoding sensitivity.

E5.justification: Appendix I newly reports pairwise inter-annotator Cohen kappa on 100 responses labeled by all six annotators, with average agreement reported as 90.5%. The existing three-run standard-deviation reporting for 26 models remains; its relocation from Figure 6 to Figure 7 is not an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Results expand to 56 models and gain new validation outcomes. Existing values also change: Figure 4 reports GPT-4o fulfillment as 0.31 in v1 versus 0.30 in v2, and Table 1 changes fine-tuned Mistral agreement from 81.3% to 81.0%. These accompany revised datasets/settings and are not demonstrated same-setting performance changes. New findings include 44.5% average maximum Jaccard similarity and 90.5% inter-annotator agreement. Some exact scores remain inconsistent within v2: Llama-Guard-2-8B is 39.0% in Table 1 but 40.8% in Table 6.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical results or proofs. v2's Equation 1 states the standard Jaccard-index formula for an empirical overlap analysis; it does not introduce a new mathematical definition or theoretical contribution.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion revise the benchmark contribution from 45 categories and 450 instructions to 44 and 440, and expand the claimed model evaluation from over 40 to over 50 models. The central claims about balanced coverage, linguistic variation and efficient small-model judges remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation and limitations. Appendix A.1 explains that refusal scores cannot establish usefulness; K.3 explicitly separates lower fulfillment from universally greater safety. J.4 discusses misleading response formatting, disclaimers and partial fulfillment as judge failure mechanisms. Additional discussion qualifies timing comparisons and acknowledges incomplete temperature coverage, beyond v1's existing limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds four-author taxonomy-consensus details, collector training and assignments, the 3,656-instruction source bank, examples for all 44 categories, exact system-prompt strings and timing parallelization details. These improve documentation, while the existing judge-training hyperparameters, hardware description and asset-access arrangements remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion concerning WildGuard, over-refusal, utility benchmarks and decoding practices. Appendix C newly juxtaposes SORRY-Bench scores with four existing safety benchmarks while cautioning against direct comparison. This extends contextual positioning without replacing the original novelty argument or related-work survey.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact. v2 shortens the title and headings, adopts open-weight terminology, adds contribution bullets, moves hosting information into a reproducibility statement, and subdivides the expanded appendices. These are localized editorial and organizational changes rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: Figure 4 is substantially redesigned and expanded from 43-by-45 to 56-by-44 entries, with category labels moved above the heatmap and revised model-label formatting. v2 adds the cross-benchmark and decoding tables, an inter-annotator heatmap, and extensive boxed examples. The conference template also reflows existing tables, figures and text.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, the annotation-agreement check, overlap analysis, judge-failure examples and decoding comparison make the benchmark more auditable, while the expanded limitations clarify what refusal scores mean. These support a net quality improvement. The gains are tempered by the unexplained removal of Impersonation coverage and conflicting evaluator scores between v2's Tables 1 and 6, which leave parts of the revised reporting less precise.
